newsitem.title: UK: International conference calls for bank law reform.
newsitem.headline: International conference calls for bank law reform.

text.p: Senior legal officials and regulators attending a conference on economic crime this week called for sweeping reform of international banking and business laws to strike at crime and corruption.
Delegates targeted banking secrecy laws and the protected status of offshore financial centres which they said have developed into havens for money laundering by organised crime.
A former advisor to British intelligence agencies MI5 and MI6 made a highly unusual and public criticism of the government for supporting offshore centres and bank secrecy laws.
David Bickford said "endemic corruption" was caused by offshore secrecy and "it is difficult to see why it is tolerated by any other than those with an unlawful disposition."
The 14th annual Cambridge International Seminar on Economic Crime is being attended by over 800 delegates from 90 countries.
U.S. lawyer George Moscarino of the firm Jones Day Reavis & Pogue in Cleveland, agreed that "money laundering profit centres are allowed to exist by mainstream nations".
"The bank secrecy laws (which protect client confidentiality) must be relaxed. There may have been justification for them decades ago, but no longer."

UK-based lawyer Arnold Rosen also considers that governments are condoning corrupt trade and business practice. "Trade, business and government are so bound up that corruption has become institutionalised," he said.

"There is a realpolitik aspect to corruption in that it enjoys wide covert government support. No government is powerful enough to ignore commercial pressures and they are unwilling to tackle obvious centres of abuse like offshore havens."
Rosen also called for a "re-think of corporate law so that each director, shareholder and employee is responsible for what they are doing."

But he noted that the decision of Swiss banks to try to trace "Hitler's millions" -- the fortunes believed to have been deposited by the Nazis in Swiss banks during World War Two -- was a "spectacular breach of the notion of banking secrecy".
"This is the first chink. We are also starting to see some action from the Council of Europe, among other institutions, which is the the first sign of a change in political will."

The third day of the week-long conference was disrupted by a suspected car-bomb next to the conference venue. Police told organisers the meeting had become a target "because of press reports making the link between organised crime and corruption".

Discussing different legal approaches to tackling corruption, Henry Rossbacher, a former U.S. Assistant Attorney in California, said the Watergate affair, which indicted former President Richard Nixon, was "a sea change in public opinion".

"It sparked the view that the Administration could not be trusted to prosecute its own," he said. "Now the trend is to criminalise the non-reporting of suspicious incidents -- it is not enough to say that you can't take a bribe, now a failure to report a bribe being offered is criminal."
In a discussion session, delegates said public opinion in many Western countries was now much more exacting on issues like corruption, corporate governance in business and environmental concerns.
Elected representatives would be under increasing pressure to disclose earnings, and political parties their donations.

Lawyer Moscarino also noted a trend in U.S. courts to punish companies without an "honesty policy" more heavily if they are caught in any wrongdoing. "If you don't have a policy you take a bigger hit. Courts are also looking at how a corporation is run, the company culture."
